summary:
Mars Survival is an interactive educational website that explores how location, equipment, and limited resources affect survival on Mars.

Users select any point on a Mars globe or flat map, configure their supplies and shelter equipment, and receive three answers: How long could they survive? What runs out first? What could help them survive longer?

The model tracks oxygen, water, food, battery energy, and solar generation for up to 120 Martian days (sols). Users can change equipment, astronaut count, season, and dust assumptions, then compare the resulting estimates. A resource timeline shows how supplies change over time.

The website also tests alternative starting locations with identical supplies. Latitude and season influence modeled sunlight, helping explain why some locations may support longer operation.

NASA imagery and MOLA elevation data provide geographic context. The website clearly separates these observations from simulation assumptions. Local temperature, extractable ice, radiation, and travel costs are not currently modeled.

Built with React, TypeScript, and Three.js, Mars Survival makes survival tradeoffs accessible through interactive exploration and plain-language explanations. It is an educational prototype, not an astronaut-safety prediction. Future work includes verified environmental data integration and model validation.
details:
Mars Survival is an interactive educational website that turns Mars exploration into a question anyone can investigate: “How long could I survive here, what would limit me, and what could help?”

What it does and how it works

Users select any location on a 3D Mars globe or flat map, then configure their astronaut count, shelter equipment, and supplies. The website models oxygen, water, food, battery energy, and solar generation for up to 120 Martian days, called sols.

The results answer three questions: How long? Why this long? What could help? Users see the number of completed sols before the first modeled failure, an explanation of the limiting resource, and suggestions for changing their setup. A timeline shows how supplies change, while before-and-after comparisons make the effects of equipment or location changes visible.

Latitude and the selected season influence modeled sunlight. The website tests alternative locations north and south of the selected point using identical starting supplies. If a tested location supports longer operation, users can preview it. These are comparisons between starting sites—not predictions of survival during travel.

Benefits and intended impact

Our goal is to make Mars survival tradeoffs understandable to students, space enthusiasts, and challenge participants without requiring specialist knowledge. Rather than presenting a map or a survival number alone, the project connects location, resources, and explanations in one experience.

Users can investigate questions such as whether additional batteries improve their estimate, how astronaut count affects supply consumption, or why changing location does not replenish food. The intended impact is to encourage scientific curiosity, systems thinking, and informed questioning of simulation results.

NASA resources

NASA Viking imagery provides the global surface visualization, and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX imagery provides detailed context around Jezero Crater. Mars Global Surveyor MOLA data supplies regional elevation readings. NASA mission-location resources support reference markers.

We distinguish these observations from our engineering assumptions. Imagery and elevation provide geographic context; they do not directly determine the survival estimate.

Tools and development

The application was developed using React and TypeScript. Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei power the interactive globe; Recharts displays resource histories; Zustand manages application state; and Lucide supplies interface icons. Vite builds the website, Vitest and React Testing Library support automated testing, and GitHub Actions deploys it to GitHub Pages. No specialist hardware is required to access the website.

OpenAI Codex assisted with development, debugging, testing, deployment, and documentation.

Creativity and design considerations

The project’s creative approach is to make a selected point on Mars the beginning of an interactive explanation. Users can change assumptions and immediately compare outcomes, connecting planetary geography with everyday concepts such as food, water, and electricity.

We prioritized clear language, visible controls, responsive layouts, coordinate-based selection, and transparent data provenance. We also considered the risk of presenting a simplified estimate as scientific certainty.

The model assumes a pressurized shelter. Local temperature, radiation, extractable ice, terrain obstacles, and travel costs are not currently integrated. Heating is a configurable assumption, and results that reach the simulation limit are labeled “At least 120 sols.”

Mars Survival is an educational prototype, not an operational astronaut-safety tool. Future work will focus on verified environmental data, model validation, uncertainty estimates, and user testing.
